home.title: Caixa-Preta: find out why your PC shut down on its own
home.description: Free, open-source hardware monitor for Windows 11. Records temperatures, power supply voltages and power draw once per second, safe against power loss, and explains the likely cause of every unexpected shutdown.

hero.titleQuestion: Did your PC shut down on its own?

whyShutdown.q: Why does my PC shut down or restart on its own?
whyShutdown.a: The most common causes are a power supply that stops delivering stable power, a CPU that overheats, a failing motherboard power stage (VRM) and a driver or Windows crash (blue screen). Windows only records that an unexpected shutdown happened (event Kernel-Power 41), not why. Caixa-Preta records the sensors continuously to show what happened in the seconds before the crash.

what.a: It records temperatures, the +12 V, +5 V and +3.3 V rails, CPU power and load, memory and NVMe disks once per second into a local database that survives power loss (SQLite in WAL mode). When the PC comes back after an unexpected shutdown, it finds the incident in the Windows Event Log and produces an explainable diagnosis of the likely cause.

cause.q: Does it tell the cause for certain?
cause.a: No. It ranks the hypotheses (power supply, overheating, motherboard, software, CPU or memory, power button) by the sum of the evidence and shows everything that counted for and against, plus the limits of the case, such as the precision of one reading per second. It is a likely cause to guide your next test, not a verdict.

free.a: Yes. It is free and open source under the MIT licence. The code, the tests and the architecture decisions are on GitHub.

privacy.q: Does my data leave the computer?
privacy.a: No. There is no cloud, no account and no telemetry. The data stays in %ProgramData%\PcMonitor and the dashboard is served only on 127.0.0.1:5280, reachable from the machine itself.

smartscreen.q: Why does Windows show a warning when I install it?
smartscreen.a: The installer is not code-signed, so SmartScreen shows "Windows protected your PC". To go on, click "More info" and then "Run anyway". Every release publishes the SHA-256 hash of the installer so you can check the file, and you can build the installer from the source code.

sensors.a: It uses LibreHardwareMonitor to read CPU temperature, load and power, the power supply rails measured by the motherboard's sensor chip, fans, memory use and NVMe disk temperatures. What shows up depends on the motherboard: when a sensor is missing, the diagnosis says so.

requirements.a: 64-bit Windows 11 and administrator rights to install. The installer carries everything it needs (no .NET required) and installs the PawnIO driver through winget if it is missing.

uninstall.q: How do I uninstall it, and what happens to the data?
uninstall.a: From Windows: Settings > Apps > Installed apps > Caixa-Preta. The uninstaller asks whether the recorded data should be deleted. Updating to a new version keeps the data.

contribute.a: Yes. Open an issue with your case or a pull request on GitHub. The project uses .NET 10 and Nuxt 4, follows a layered architecture checked by architecture tests and records every decision in an ADR.

recorder.title: The seconds Windows does not keep
recorder.lead: After an unexpected shutdown, Windows only records that it happened. Caixa-Preta keeps what came before.
recorder.chartLabel: The +12 V rail in the 40 seconds before the crash: steady at 12.10 V, then sagging below 11.40 V, the bottom of the ATX range

recording.title: Recording
recording.text: One reading per second of temperature, load, power and voltages, saved to a database that survives a power cut.

crash.title: The crash
crash.text: Under a game load, the +12 V rail sags for 40 seconds and leaves the ATX range. The screen goes dark.

restart.title: Back on
restart.text: Two minutes later the PC is back. Caixa-Preta finds the shutdown in the Windows Event Log.

diagnosis.title: Diagnosis
diagnosis.text: The rules weigh what was recorded against each possible cause and show why.

verdict.label: Most likely cause
verdict.for: The +12 V rail was below 11.40 V in more than one reading
verdict.for2: The CPU was under heavy load, drawing more power
verdict.against: The CPU was at 71 °C, far from its limit: not overheating
verdict.against2: No blue screen was recorded: not Windows
verdict.limit: The sensor sits on the motherboard: it cannot tell the power supply from the board or the connector.

features.title: What it does
features.lead: Everything runs on your machine, in three processes with the least privilege each needs.

recording.title: Recording that survives power loss
recording.text: Temperatures, load, power, the +12 V, +5 V and +3.3 V rails, fans, memory and NVMe disks, once per second, in SQLite with WAL. The last seconds before the power goes are on disk.

detection.title: Every unexpected shutdown
detection.text: It reads the Windows Event Log (Kernel-Power 41 and related events) and ties each crash to its stretch of the recording.

diagnosis.title: Explainable diagnosis
diagnosis.text: Power supply, motherboard, overheating, software, CPU or memory, power button: each hypothesis scores by the evidence, and you see everything that counted.

mini.title: Always-on-top mini panel
mini.text: A small strip above your other windows. The numbers turn red when something leaves its normal range.

export.title: Export it for your technician
export.text: History and incidents as CSV, Excel or PDF.

privacy.title: Nothing leaves the machine
privacy.text: No cloud, account or telemetry. The dashboard only answers on 127.0.0.1.

engineering.title: Built to last and to be read

story.quote: Caixa-Preta was born because of my cat.
story.text: He is a big cat, and he climbed onto the PC case to jump on top of the wardrobe. When he jumped, the case did not stay on the desk: it fell more than 80 cm. From then on the PC kept restarting on its own, and I could not tell whether the motherboard or the power supply was at fault. I wanted to monitor the voltages to find out.
story.author: Gabriel Silva, author
story.illustration: Animated illustration: the cat sits on the PC case on the desk and leaps onto the wardrobe; the push knocks the case off the 80 cm desk, and its power light keeps blinking as the PC restarts.
